transferablePrinciples: Use bold, repeated section separators to make a long storefront feel chunked into manageable accessory families.
Alternate low-density editorial modules with high-density commerce modules so shoppers can understand a family before facing broad assortment choice.
Introduce a key innovation or hero accessory with a short proof-story sequence before presenting purchase options.
Bridge from storytelling to shopping with a small curated feature matrix before dropping into a full native product grid.
Keep editorial and native commerce visually distinct: use lifestyle photography and simplified copy for story modules, then let standard buyable cards handle comparison shopping.
Reuse one section architecture across multiple families to create predictability in very long pages.
Anchor section hero images with a small informational plaque rather than heavy copy overlays, preserving image impact while still labeling the family.
Let native product cards do the detailed selling work; surrounding modules should focus on orientation, context, and prioritization rather than duplicating card metadata.
Use occasional cross-category promo banners near the end of long assortment pages to provide onward navigation without interrupting main shopping earlier.
Preserve generous white space in featured-product modules so hero items feel premium, then accept tighter density in the broader catalog area.
designerInstructions: Create a full-width brand opener with one environmental photograph, oversized brand-weight headline text, and minimal supporting copy.
Use full-width category divider bands with centered high-weight typography to mark each major accessory family.
For the lead family, build an editorial proof block with one short intro text area and three equal visual cards showing the product in use; keep copy concise and image-led.

Translate the lead family into a curated product matrix on white: one narrative text tile plus several single-product feature tiles with strong name-first hierarchy and small compatibility/support copy beneath.
Show product cutouts isolated on clean backgrounds in featured tiles; place them off-center so the layout has negative space instead of feeling like a catalog grid.
If including a video, treat the poster as a full-width lifestyle image with a centered play affordance; do not rely on motion to carry the layout.
For repeatable accessory families, pair each section title band with one full-width hero image and a small top-left overlay plaque containing a label and a one-sentence description.
Reserve native product grids for breadth: keep editorial imagery out of the card area so shoppers can quickly compare many SKUs.
Group long assortments by family rather than mixing unrelated products into one uninterrupted grid.
When moving from one family to the next, use a strong visual reset: bold divider band, then one large image, then the product grid.
End the page with compact cross-navigation banners to adjacent categories and a low-emphasis utility/footer area.
Apply these patterns using the destination brand's own color system, typography, imagery style, and assortment logic rather than copying the source brand's visual identity.

transferablePrinciples: Open with one broad campaign-quality hero that shows the product in context before narrowing into a specific subcategory or use case.
Use a repeatable chapter-bar device to divide a long page into clear thematic sections without adding heavy navigation.
Place a short, centered explainer block early on to frame the product benefit in plain language before presenting buying UI.
Follow explanatory copy with an editorial collage that combines lifestyle usage, detail shots, and an isolated product image in one composed feature.
Transition from custom storytelling into a native buyable module once the shopper has enough context; let the native module handle specs, price, ratings, and purchase actions.
Keep the main product section singular and focused when the page is built around one hero SKU, rather than diluting attention with many parallel options.
Use accessory content as a secondary chapter after the main conversion moment, with lighter emphasis and fewer competing choices.
Reserve strong contrast blocks for section titles and hero claims, while leaving white space around detailed commerce modules so they remain legible.
Differentiate editorial imagery from native commerce clearly: custom collages should look intentionally composed, while buyable items should retain recognizable marketplace UI patterns.
End with a low-priority utility/footer action rather than extending the sales narrative indefinitely.
designerInstructions: Create a full-width opening hero using real lifestyle photography of the product in use; place one short, high-weight headline directly on the image and keep supporting store navigation in a separate, thinner strip below.
Introduce each major chapter with a simple horizontal title band that spans the full content width and contains only one centered label.
Use a white-background intro block with one oversized centered paragraph and a single restrained CTA beneath it; avoid cluttering this section with extra badges or secondary links.
Build the main editorial feature as an asymmetrical collage: one tall human-use image, one or two smaller supporting detail images, and one text-led panel containing an isolated product render.
Weight text unevenly inside the collage: one dominant headline, one short supporting line, and one compact CTA overlay; do not let every panel compete equally.
Layer content mostly through panel adjacency and contrast, not through heavy shadows, cards, or deep overlap effects.
After the editorial story, insert a native buyable product module so shoppers can switch from inspiration to purchase without leaving the page narrative.
Ensure the native commerce module visibly contrasts with the editorial area by using cleaner isolation, standard product media behavior, and denser factual text.
For accessories, use a quieter split layout with brief explanatory text on one side and one or a few native add-on products on the other; keep this section subordinate to the main SKU.
Use spacious vertical transitions between modules so each chapter feels deliberate; separate story, commerce, and add-on moments with clear visual resets rather than subtle shifts alone.
If using product part imagery for accessories, treat it as a native product card or packshot, not as an editorial still life, unless the goal is storytelling rather than direct purchase.
Finish with a minimal utility/footer action centered in generous whitespace so the page ends cleanly.

transferablePrinciples: Use the top of the page to establish category context quickly: lifestyle hero first, then a hard section label, then a concise explanation of what the range covers.

designerInstructions: Open with a wide editorial hero photograph that shows the product in active use in a believable environment. Keep any overlaid text secondary to the image.

Show the assortment next as one grouped product composition on a clean background. Treat it as a family portrait, not as a retail grid. If the platform allows shopping markers, keep them discreet.
Build supporting editorial sections as a two-column mosaic mixing text-only tiles, staged ownership scenes, and real usage photography. Use the text-only tiles to pace the image flow.

Editorial feature tiles should use either in-use photography or close-up detail shots. Add short, benefit-led labels inside simple corner boxes with strong contrast against the image.
Keep grouping logic stable as the shopper scrolls: overview divider, product-feature cluster, next divider, next cluster. The repetition should aid comparison rather than feel monotonous.
As the page moves downward, allow retail density to increase, but preserve generous gutters and white space so native pricing and product details remain scannable.
Close with cross-sell tiles that are simpler and louder than the product grid: bold headings, compact product cutouts, and button-like onward CTAs.

transferablePrinciples: Structure a category page as a progression from context, to range overview, to subtype routing, to direct shopping.
Use one unmistakable category naming device early in the page so shoppers immediately understand what the section covers.
When the assortment contains multiple form factors, start with a simplified editorial lineup that compares silhouettes or categories without transactional clutter.
Separate editorial navigation tiles from native shoppable product cards so category exploration and direct purchase feel like different stages.
Keep subcategory tiles visually consistent through fixed aspect ratios, repeated label placement, and repeated image logic even when subject matter changes.
Let real-use photography explain use cases, while reserve native marketplace cards for detailed price-and-purchase information.

Maintain a clear rhythm of spacious editorial moments alternating with denser functional commerce zones.
designerInstructions: Open with a wide lifestyle image that shows the category in a believable usage environment. Keep this masthead visually broad and relatively shallow in height.
Place a single high-weight category heading in a full-width color band immediately after navigation so the page purpose is obvious at a glance.
Build an editorial hero on a light or neutral background using several representative products isolated as a grouped composition. Space them evenly and avoid turning this into a card grid.
Keep hero copy minimal in the lineup section. If a CTA is needed, make it small and unobtrusive so the product silhouettes remain the primary message.
Create a rigid subcategory grid with repeated tile dimensions. Use photographic tiles, not icons, and attach short high-contrast labels consistently to one edge of each image.
Mix environments across the tile grid to express use cases: workshop, vehicle, home, specialist task, accessory detail, and similar scenarios relevant to the assortment.
Insert a centered sentence or short paragraph as a visual reset before moving into transactional content.
Announce the shopping section with another strong divider band so the shift from browsing to buying is explicit.
Use a wide editorial banner above the native product list, and place copy in a contained overlay card rather than spreading text directly across the full photo.
Rely on native marketplace product cards for the buyable assortment. Do not redesign pricing, ratings, or purchase controls into custom editorial boxes.
Expect the native product area to be visually denser; manage this by surrounding it with simpler modules before and after.
For cross-sell, use a small number of broad promo panels with product cutouts, concise category naming, and clearly separated CTA buttons.
Keep layering shallow across the page: mostly flat blocks, with only occasional overlay cards or floating buttons to create emphasis.

designerInstructions: Create a wide desktop hero using one strong automotive-interior cleaning action photo. Keep the crop broad and immersive, with the product visibly in use.

observations: The topmost strip is a wide lifestyle hero showing the product in use on a car, cropped as a panoramic banner rather than a product detail image.
A turquoise endorsement-style badge with a very large numeral sits over the hero image at right, creating the strongest layered element in the header.
Below the hero is a narrow white store-navigation row with brand mark, follow/share utility controls, multiple text tabs, and a right-aligned search field.
The range title appears in a full-width bright yellow band with heavy black display lettering centered in the strip.
The introductory copy sits alone on white, center-aligned, using large type and generous blank space around it.
The first product-focused section uses two oversized isolated machine cutouts on white; this is a photographed/retouched composition, not a native product grid.
A small dark pill-shaped CTA appears low on the left in the isolated product stage, visually subordinate to the packshots.
The editorial feature area uses an alternating checkerboard: text block opposite image, then image opposite text, maintaining rhythm without needing dividers.
One lifestyle image shows the machine stored in an open car trunk alongside everyday items, supporting the portability message through visible scale context.
Another lifestyle image shows a person cleaning a motorcycle; the product itself is secondary to the action and ease-of-use scenario.
The next checkerboard repeats the same logic with outdoor cleaning and home storage scenes, keeping visual continuity across separate benefits.
The storage photo places the product on a shelf among boots, bins, and boxed items, making organization a visible proof point rather than an abstract claim.
The comparison sections are compressed full-width bands with tiny spec rows and small pictograms; the detailed microcopy is difficult to read at the provided strip resolution.
Both product-assortment areas are mixed compositions rather than uniform catalog grids: native buyable cards are interrupted by one larger editorial tile.
Native product cards use clean white backgrounds, product packshots, text title/subtitle stacks, and price lines; they visually read as Amazon commerce units rather than custom-designed story cards.
The editorial tile inside the first product mosaic uses a deck-cleaning lifestyle photo with a headline overlay, visually larger and more atmospheric than the neighboring product cards.
The editorial tile inside the second product mosaic uses a garden cleaning scene with a white text box overlay, creating stronger contrast than plain text directly on the image.
The endcap section uses two side-by-side yellow promo banners, each with a strong CTA block; one also includes a small lineup image placed near the lower portion of the banner.
The final visible section is not empty content space; it contains a centered share control and a short helper line, so the page remains functionally finished rather than abruptly cut off.
No visible video poster or playback control is present in the supplied strips.
transferablePrinciples: Use a broad store-context header, then immediately switch into a range-specific visual system so shoppers understand they are inside a focused assortment story.
Open a range page with a simple section banner and a short centered positioning statement before introducing technical or transactional content.
Give the hero product family a dedicated white stage with oversized isolated packshots when compactness, form factor, or accessory layout needs to be immediately legible.
Translate functional benefits into alternating image-and-text checkerboards so each claim is paired with visual proof from a real environment.
Keep editorial feature copy short and centered when the photography already explains the scenario; avoid long paragraphs that compete with the images.
Insert compact comparison separators before commerce sections to help shoppers mentally segment model tiers without overwhelming the page with dense tables everywhere.
Blend native product cards with occasional editorial tiles so the page remains buyable without collapsing into a monotonous catalog grid.
Use editorial tiles inside product mosaics to communicate use-case breadth, accessory ecosystems, or situational relevance that standard commerce cards cannot show alone.
End focused product sections with adjacent-category promos to catch shoppers who may need a different tier or supporting consumables.
Maintain consistent gutters, repeated module widths, and predictable alternation patterns so a long page feels structured even when content types change.
designerInstructions: Start with a wide lifestyle banner cropped horizontally, showing the product in active use within a recognizable real-world setting.
Place a compact utility/navigation strip directly under the hero; keep it visually quieter than the hero so it frames rather than competes.
Use one bold full-width color band as the range title marker, with a single heavy display line centered inside it.
Follow with a centered introductory statement on a white background; use large type, light wording, and generous margins.
Create an oversized white product stage using isolated cutout or retouched packshot imagery. Use few words and let silhouette, accessories, and scale do the work.

Build feature storytelling as alternating two-column blocks: one side short centered copy, the other side a lifestyle photo that proves the claim. Reverse left/right positions in the next row to create rhythm.
Choose editorial photos that show the product in context with surrounding objects, surfaces, or storage spaces so viewers can judge size, portability, and setup intuitively.
Keep layering restrained. Most sections should feel flat and clean; use overlays only when an editorial image needs a stronger headline container for legibility.
Introduce model-family transitions with shallow comparison bands that use graphic blocks, small icons, and brief data clusters rather than long explanatory text.
For shoppable areas, mix native commerce cards with one editorial tile per grid so transactional units are softened by one image-led storytelling moment.
On native product cards, keep the hierarchy simple: product name strongest, supporting descriptor next, transactional line after. Let packshots stay on plain backgrounds for clarity.
For endcap navigation, use bold promo tiles with a clear category label and a prominent button-style CTA; optional small product imagery can help distinguish one destination from another.
Finish with a light utility footer rather than a visually heavy closing section, so the main product content remains the page climax.

pages.pageRole: Brand store landing page that first explains a shared 18 V battery ecosystem, then merchandises compatible batteries, chargers, and a larger set of buyable platform devices.
observations: The very top image is a close crop of a hand inserting or handling a battery on a yellow outdoor tool; only a fragment of the tool is shown, which creates immediate focus on battery interaction rather than the full product.
Store navigation sits directly under the top image and includes many links plus a search field, but the page-specific content begins visually with a strong full-width title band.
The title band uses very large black all-caps text centered on a bright solid background, creating a clear sectional anchor.
The intro section contains only centered black text on a very light neutral background, with large line spacing and no adjacent CTA or image, making it intentionally airy.

In the split editorial feature, the left image is a clean isolated battery render on a pale surface, while the right image is a darker poster-like square showing a battery centered in a circular ring of many tiny device silhouettes.
A visible play icon sits over the right square poster, so it should be treated as a video poster or media tile rather than assumed static-only artwork.
A small black technical badge with yellow iconography appears between/above the split images, adding a compact feature cue without becoming a full card.
The second explanatory paragraph again uses centered text-only presentation, reinforcing the page's rhythm of 'headline/explanation -> image focus -> explanation -> shopping'.
The accessory subsection title appears in another full-width high-contrast band, visually matching the page title structure but at a smaller scale.

The mixed battery/charger area is not a standard uniform native grid: some tiles are buyable product cards with prices, while others are editorial tiles about features such as display readouts, internal cell technology, and wall mounting.
In the mixed grid, native product cards often use small cutout packshots and text blocks placed beside or above them instead of the deeper metadata stack seen later in the full Amazon grid.
One editorial feature tile shows an enlarged battery close-up with a white text box label placed over the image area, rather than keeping text entirely outside the image.
Another editorial tile uses an exploded-view style image of battery internals laid out horizontally on a pale background, which visually conveys engineering detail without lifestyle context.
The wall-mount editorial tile uses an in-context installed product photograph with cable visible, contrasting with the cutout packshots used in adjacent shoppable cards.
The 'product highlights' divider repeats the same bold banner convention, making major sections easy to scan.

The large assortment hero beneath it is a photographed multi-product composition, not a native grid: multiple tools are staged together on grass and patio in front of a wood-slat wall, with a white copy panel overlay at left.
The full native product area switches to a clear five-column desktop grid, each card on white with consistent image-to-text structure and standardized bottom CTA placement.
Within the native grid, some product cards end in filled yellow CTA bars while others use lighter outline-style buttons, indicating mixed purchase paths within the same grid.
Ratings stars, review counts, strike-through/discount formatting, shipping lines, and CTA buttons are all visible in the native product cards, making this the densest information zone on the page.
The native grid extends for several rows and ends with a centered 'show more' style button, signaling additional browsing depth.
Below the grid are two bright promotional banners placed side by side; both are clearly navigational/brand-promotional rather than direct purchase cards.
The final visible section is a small centered share utility with a rounded button and short helper text, so the page does not end directly on product cards.

No blank intentional spacer dominates the layout, but some DOM-reported tile areas are visually ambiguous in the screenshot because repeated editorial tiling is abstracted into larger composed sections rather than individually legible cells.
transferablePrinciples: Use a top-of-page sequence that moves from brand context to a single unmistakable platform title before asking the user to process shopping options.
Alternate high-whitespace explanatory sections with image-led sections to keep technical ecosystem messaging readable and not overly dense.
When explaining a shared battery or compatibility platform, show both the core power unit in close detail and the broader family of compatible devices in one visual story.
Separate major content shifts with strong full-width section dividers so users can instantly understand when the page moves from explanation to component shopping to full assortment browsing.
Mix editorial benefit tiles with buyable component cards when a category needs education before conversion, but keep the visual distinction clear.

Use different image modes for different jobs: isolated packshots for shoppable clarity, staged multi-product photography for ecosystem breadth, and technical diagrams/in-context installs for feature education.
Introduce the full assortment with a staged hero composition before dropping into a dense native product grid; this preserves brand storytelling while still supporting conversion.
Keep upper-page copy concise and centered when the concept is simple, then let native commerce modules carry the heavier details later.
Allow card-level asymmetry in smaller mixed sections to avoid a monotonous grid, but switch to a uniform grid for broad assortment scanning.
End long commerce pages with cross-navigation promos and a lightweight utility/footer action to extend exploration without forcing more products.
designerInstructions: Start with a cropped usage photograph that shows the platform's power component being handled or inserted into a device; do not require the whole product to be visible if the interaction is clear.
Follow with a full-width title band using one oversized headline and no competing elements.
Place a large centered introductory statement on a light neutral field with generous margins and no CTA.

Build a split editorial module: one side should be a large isolated render or clean product photograph of the core power component; the other side should be a poster-style ecosystem visual or video poster showing the platform's wider compatibility range. If using media, show only the poster frame and play cue unless playback is explicit.
Add a short centered explanatory paragraph before the first shopping section to explain how the assortment is organized.

For the first commerce section, mix native buyable product cards with non-buyable editorial feature tiles. Use native cards for core SKUs and editorial tiles for compatibility, technology, mounting, care, or internal-component stories.

Keep text weighting simple in mixed sections: product name first, one short support line second, transactional data last. Editorial tiles should use a short feature label plus one brief descriptor only.
Group smaller products in a two-column or mosaic layout with enough white space that editorial tiles can breathe; vary image alignment left/right across cards to prevent visual fatigue.

Use at least one photographed multi-product composition before the large grid to stage the wider family together in a single aspirational or contextual scene. Overlay text in a separate panel rather than embedding all copy into the background image.

Transition into the full native product grid with uniform card sizing, consistent gutters, and standardized CTA placement. Let native Amazon card structure handle ratings, price, and availability rather than recreating those editorially.
After the dense grid, place a pair of promotional banners for adjacent ranges or related categories. Treat them as navigational blocks with bold category naming and a distinct CTA zone.
Close with a minimal utility area such as share/help/follow rather than another heavy visual section.

pages.pageRole: Accessory and consumables cross-sell catalog for existing vacuum and wash-vac owners, guiding them to compatible replacement filters, tools, and cleaning solutions with direct product tiles and a few category jump-offs.
observations: A full-width hero photo at the top shows a person using a canister-style vacuum in an unfinished interior; the image spans edge to edge and is visually separate from the shopping grid below.

Directly under the hero, a slim navigation/header bar contains brand/store navigation and a search field; this bar is much smaller than the merchandising content and functions as infrastructure rather than promotion.
The main section title sits inside a full-width, saturated color band and is set in very large, bold, uppercase black text centered horizontally.

Most of the body content sits on white or very light off-white tiles arranged in two equal desktop columns with wide gutters; tile borders are subtle or effectively invisible, so spacing defines the grid.
Section opener tiles frequently contain only centered bold copy with no product image, acting as editorial signposts inside the grid.

Native buyable products are not shown as a conventional dense Amazon shelf; instead they appear one-up or two-up inside oversized editorial tiles with title, short explanatory text, price, and a cutout packshot.

Packshots are usually positioned toward the outer edge of the tile, leaving the center or inner side for the text block; some show packaging plus accessory/tool, while others show only the component itself.

Several full-bleed lifestyle images interrupt the white product matrix: one under a sofa/floor-cleaning scene, one close-up of car-seat/upholstery cleaning, and smaller in-grid use photos for handheld/cordless attachments.
There are no visible star ratings, review summaries, or dense badge clusters in the product area; the visible emphasis is on compatibility/use description and price rather than social proof.
The bottom promotional area changes style noticeably: two adjacent solid-color tiles include device illustrations and rectangular CTA-button shapes, unlike the white native product tiles above.

transferablePrinciples: Use a small number of recurring desktop modules rather than a fully custom layout for every section: hero, title band, two-column product matrix, full-width divider, category CTA, utility footer.
Separate product families with editorial reset moments. A full-width lifestyle image can effectively break up repetitive native product rows and signal a new use case or device ecosystem.
Embed native buyable products inside a branded editorial grid instead of isolating them in a pure shelf. This keeps direct purchase possible while preserving brand storytelling.
Use text-only intro tiles to explain compatibility or usage themes before showing products. These tiles help orient owners of different device lines without requiring long paragraphs.
Let product imagery stay simple and technical when the buying task is compatibility-driven: isolated packshots on clean backgrounds make accessories and replacement parts easier to parse.
Alternate between single-feature emphasis and paired product comparison. One-up tiles can highlight a lead item or section opener; two-up rows can efficiently cover closely related accessories.
Reserve heavier visual drama for transitions, not every tile. Panoramic in-use photos work best as section dividers or proof points between clusters of white catalog tiles.
Use broader category CTA tiles at the end of an accessory page to catch shoppers who may actually need the base device family rather than another add-on.
Keep copy hierarchy disciplined: section statement first, product name second, compatibility/use note third, commercial details last.
Design the module system so it can accept varying numbers of products; the structure should scale without depending on a fixed SKU count.
designerInstructions: Build the page on a desktop two-column canvas with generous gutters and large rectangular tiles. Use a few repeatable module types and keep the rhythm consistent across the full scroll.
Open with one wide lifestyle image that shows the core device in use in a believable environment. Keep text on this image minimal or absent so the photo establishes context quickly.
Follow the hero with a single, high-contrast section title band. The title should be the heaviest text on the page and act as a visual threshold into shopping content.
For the main body, create oversized white tiles that can hold either: a text-only section statement, one native product card, two side-by-side native product cards, or a full-bleed editorial photo.
When using native product cards, keep the copy block compact and compatibility-oriented. Weight the product name first, a short use/fit line second, and price or commerce details last.
Place cutout product images against very clean backgrounds with plenty of breathing room. Push packshots toward the outer edge of the tile so the inner area can hold readable text.

Use photographed multi-product compositions only for navigational or promotional tiles, not for standard buyable accessory tiles. Standard accessory tiles should read as native products, not ad collages.
Insert full-width or half-width lifestyle photos between product clusters to reset attention. These images should show the accessory or tool in use, with tight crops and clear surface/context cues.
Keep layering shallow. Avoid decorative frames, heavy shadows, or complex overlays; rely on alignment, white space, and scale contrast to separate modules.

Use a final pair of category promo tiles to redirect shoppers into adjacent device families. These can be more graphic and button-led than the main product matrix, but they should still fit the overall modular system.
End with a low-emphasis utility strip rather than another sales block so users can tell the merchandising journey has concluded.

pages.pageRole: Category landing page for irrigation that orients shoppers, showcases use cases, and drives them into individual buyable products and adjacent irrigation-related ranges.
observations: The topmost visual is a wide editorial photo shot from a low angle through foliage; leaves, peppers, butterflies, and water droplets frame a person holding a watering tool against the sky.
The navigation/search bar sits directly under that photo and visually behaves like a store-wide utility layer rather than part of the irrigation content.
The page title appears in a full-width bright accent band with a single oversized black word centered, creating an immediate category signpost.
The main overview module is not a native product grid; it is a rendered or heavily composited house-and-garden scene showing multiple irrigation situations at once.
Circular hotspot markers are distributed across the overview lawn, beds, façade, and near the pool, indicating item-level discovery inside the scenic composition.
A dark rounded CTA sits at the lower left of the overview scene; no conventional product card is visible in that hero area.
Each subcategory starts with the same full-width accent banner and bold black title, creating a repeated section-divider pattern down the page.
The first three content sections use a consistent 2x2 checkerboard: two white native product cards and two editorial feature tiles.
Native product cards are easy to distinguish because they place isolated product packshots on clean white, include price lines, and sometimes show availability text in red.
Editorial feature tiles use in-use photography or macro detail imagery with a pale or semi-opaque text panel pinned near the top-left corner.
In the sprinkler section, one editorial tile is an extreme close-up of a yellow control element on a nozzle, while another shows water spray across a lawn at sunset-like light.
The watering-wand section mixes a near-blank white product stage with two people-in-garden action photos, demonstrating that the same visual system can hold both sparse and busy imagery.
The spray-nozzle section becomes much taller and more catalogue-like, using repeated two-column rows instead of a single checkerboard.
Within that longer section, the pattern alternates between product-only cards and lifestyle proof tiles, including close hand-held spraying shots and broader garden scenes.
Several cards show red availability notices, reinforcing that the products are native commerce elements rather than purely designed static brochures.
The hoses/accessories section repeats the long two-column row logic, with isolated coils and hardware contrasted against outdoor storage or transport imagery near vehicles and lawns.
The garden-shower section breaks the row rhythm: a single tall isolated shower product occupies the whole left side while the right side stacks two child-in-use lifestyle tiles.
The final promotional band uses two equal-width blocks with strong buttons, then the page ends with a centered share control on a plain white background; no further visual content is visible below.
transferablePrinciples: Open with one mood-setting brand image before product selling begins, so the page feels like a branded destination rather than only a catalogue.
Use a single, unmistakable category title band early to reset context after global navigation.
Include one overview scene that shows the whole solution ecosystem in context before breaking into subcategories.
Separate subcategories with consistent full-width divider bars that are visually stronger than body content.
Pair isolated native product cards with adjacent editorial proof tiles so shoppers can connect object-level purchase options to real usage benefits.

Repeat a small number of layout systems across the page: a compact checkerboard for hero subcategories, denser two-column rows for deeper assortment, and one asymmetrical spotlight layout for a hero item.
Keep overlay copy on imagery short and consistently placed inside readable panels rather than scattering text freely across photos.
Let native product cards carry transactional information while editorial tiles carry explanation, emotion, and feature demonstration.
Use large areas of neutral space around isolated products to keep dense assortments scannable.
End the page with cross-sell navigation to adjacent needs and a low-priority utility/footer zone rather than another dense assortment block.
designerInstructions: Start with a wide editorial hero image that shows the category in action, using foreground framing elements and visible environment depth rather than a flat packshot collage.
Follow with a single full-width category title band using your own brand typography and accent color, keeping the headline much heavier than any surrounding text.
Build one overview module as a scenic composition of the full use environment; if interactive markers are available, place them directly on meaningful zones of the scene.
For early subcategories, use a 2x2 grid where two tiles are native buyable product cards on clean white and two tiles are editorial feature images with short overlay captions.
On native product cards, isolate the product clearly, keep the name as the first readable text, and push price/availability lower in the hierarchy.
On editorial tiles, use lifestyle or macro-detail photography, add a light text panel for contrast, and keep copy concise so the image remains primary.
When the assortment becomes broader, switch to repeated two-column rows that alternate product-only cards with in-use imagery to maintain rhythm and reduce monotony.
Introduce one asymmetric module near the end to spotlight a hero or seasonal item: one large product stage on one side, stacked contextual imagery on the other.
Use consistent gutters and abrupt but orderly transitions between modules; the divider bar should feel like a hard chapter break, while the image styles inside a chapter can alternate.
Finish with two simple cross-sell banners and a quiet utility/footer strip so the page lands cleanly instead of ending inside a dense product grid.

Group product cards in an even desktop grid with tight inter-card spacing. Accept that the final row may be partially filled; maintain alignment rather than inventing filler graphics.
